# Optimized split centers: projective facet cost and one common cap transport

This note concerns one actual midpoint contact between parallel faces.
It proves a sharp total-cost bound, including the tangent continuation
of the projective density, and retains one physical coupling for every
ambient cap. It does not bound the cap-dependent defect uniformly, nor
assert a global mixed-integer descent or a selection over infinitely
many normal directions.

## 1. Statement and actual split-center freedom

Fix d>=2, k=d-1, and delta>0. Define

 f(s)=s^(-d)                                  for s>=delta,
 f(s)=delta^(-d)-d delta^(-d-1)(s-delta)       for s<=delta.

This function is positive, decreasing, convex and C1 on all of R. Put

 q(s)=-f'(s)/d=max(s,delta)^(-d-1),
 R(s)=f(s)/q(s)
     =s                         for s>=delta,
     =(d+1)delta-ds             for s<=delta.              (1)

Let F_A,F_B be compact convex k-dimensional bodies in parallel affine
hyperplanes, and let F_K be a compact convex k-dimensional body in their
midpoint plane containing (F_A+F_B)/2. All face measures below are the
intrinsic Euclidean H_k measures. Fix a vector a and a point y, and assume

 L_K(m)=1+a.(m-y)>=delta for every m in F_K.                 (2)

For a scalar t define

 L_A^t(x)=1+a.(x-y)-t,
 L_B^t(x')=1+a.(x'-y)+t,

 A(t)=integral_(F_A) f(L_A^t),
 B(t)=integral_(F_B) f(L_B^t),
 M=integral_(F_K) f(L_K).

The scalar assertion is

              min_(t in R) [A(t)+B(t)] <= 2M.             (3)

The minimum is attained. At every minimizing t, there is a SINGLE
coupling of F_A,F_B described below, and a measure zeta on F_K, such that

 zeta <= f(L_K) H_k|F_K,
 zeta(F_K)=[A(t)+B(t)]/2.                                 (4)

Its endpoint marginals are proportional to q, not to f. Formula (4)
retains the effective denominators R from (1) and is stronger than the
total-cost inequality (3).

If a!=0, every scalar shift is an ACTUAL split-center choice:

 c_A=y+t a/||a||^2,  c_B=y-t a/||a||^2,

so c_A+c_B=2y and L_A^t=1+a.(x-c_A), L_B^t=1+a.(x'-c_B).
The centers need not belong to the input bodies. If a=0, varying centers
does not create this scalar freedom: the geometric split-center theorem
is expressly restricted to a!=0. The scalar analytic theorem (3) still
has its stated meaning with independently allowed denominator offsets.

All pairs satisfy the actual identity

 L_K((x+x')/2)=[L_A^t(x)+L_B^t(x')]/2>=delta.               (5)

In particular negative endpoint denominators are permitted; they are
handled by f's tangent branch rather than discarded.

## 2. Attainment and equal derivative mass

The integrands and their first derivatives are continuous and uniformly
bounded on each compact face for t in a compact interval. Dominated
differentiation gives

 A'(t)=d integral_(F_A)q(L_A^t),
 B'(t)=-d integral_(F_B)q(L_B^t).                           (6)

Thus A+B is C1 and convex. As t tends to positive infinity, every
L_A^t enters the affine lower branch, and A(t) tends linearly to infinity
because |F_A|>0. As t tends to negative infinity, B(t) does likewise.
Hence A+B is coercive and attains its minimum. At any minimizer t*,

 J:=integral_(F_A)q(L_A^t*)
   =integral_(F_B)q(L_B^t*)>0.                             (7)

From here on omit t* from the notation. No assertion of uniqueness is
needed. The equality of the two derivative masses is essential: it is
not the equality of the endpoint costs A and B.

## 3. The scalar midpoint inequality including continuation

For all real x,y with (x+y)/2>=delta,

 f((x+y)/2)
 [(q(x)^(-1/k)+q(y)^(-1/k))/2]^k
                 >=[R(x)+R(y)]/2.                         (8)

Proof. Write p=(d+1)/k>1. If x,y>=delta, the power-mean inequality gives

 [(x^p+y^p)/2]^k >=[(x+y)/2]^(d+1).

Multiplication by [(x+y)/2]^(-d) proves (8).
Otherwise relabel so x<=delta<=y. Put z=(delta+y)/2 and
s=(delta-x)/2. Then z-s=(x+y)/2>=delta>0, and

 [(delta^p+y^p)/2]^k >= z^(d+1).

Consequently the left side of (8) is at least

 z^(d+1)/(z-s)^d=z(1-s/z)^(-d)>=z+ds,

by convexity of (1-u)^(-d) above its tangent at u=0. The final quantity
is exactly [(d+1)delta-dx+y]/2=[R(x)+R(y)]/2. If both x,y<=delta,
the assumed mean forces x=y=delta, already covered. This proves (8).

## 4. Weighted triangular transport, with a direct justification

Identify the three parallel planes by one common orthonormal tangent
coordinate system. Affine offsets are retained in L_A,L_B,L_K; intrinsic
volume in each plane becomes ordinary Lebesgue volume in R^k.

We first record the conditional-quantile construction for a compact
convex k-body F with a strictly positive continuous density w on F.
Let J_F=integral_F w. For i<k and an interior projection prefix p put

 W_i(p)=integral_{z:(p,z) in F} w(p,z) dz,
 W_0=J_F,  W_k=w on int F.

Each conditional fiber over an interior projection is a positive-volume
convex body. These fibers vary continuously in the Hausdorff metric at
interior projection points: upper inclusion follows by compactness;
for lower inclusion, first move a given fiber point slightly toward an
interior lift of that prefix, and then vary the prefix inside its small
ambient interior ball. This proves lower approximation of every point.
Their boundaries have measure zero. Dominated convergence on a fixed
bounding box therefore makes W_i continuous and positive. The same
argument for truncated fibers proves continuity of every conditional
CDF. Alternatively it follows by integrating the continuous positive
W_i along the conditional interval.

The possible ith coordinates at a fixed preceding interior prefix form
an open interval with finite continuous endpoint functions (the lower
one is convex, the upper one concave). The conditional CDF has positive
continuous own-coordinate derivative W_i/W_(i-1), and increases from
zero to one. Its inverse defines, recursively, a continuous triangular
map T_F:(0,1)^k -> int F. Its own-coordinate derivatives are positive,
continuous, and obey

 partial_i T_(F,i)=W_(i-1)(T_(F,<i))/W_i(T_(F,<=i)),
 product_i partial_i T_(F,i)=J_F/w(T_F).                    (9)

Triangular inversion is continuous by monotone bracketing on compact
subintervals. Repeated one-dimensional substitution and Tonelli give,
for every nonnegative Borel h,

 integral_F h(x)w(x)dx/J_F
                    =integral_((0,1)^k)h(T_F(r))dr.        (10)

No cross-coordinate differentiability or global multivariate area
formula is used. The boundary of a convex body has Lebesgue measure
zero, so its exclusion changes no marginal mass.

Apply this construction to w_A=q(L_A) and w_B=q(L_B), whose total
masses agree by (7). They are positive continuous functions bounded
above and below on the compact faces. Denote the maps by X(r),Y(r),
and set Z(r)=[X(r)+Y(r)]/2. This is one coupling, independent of any cap.
Its midpoint map is injective and triangular: at the first differing
coordinate, both endpoint maps strictly increase. Its diagonal
derivatives are (partial_i X_i+partial_i Y_i)/2>0.

The image G of Z is an open recursive-interval domain. Its interval
endpoints are averages of the endpoint maps' continuous conditional
endpoints, expressed through the preceding inverse prefix. Thus the
same repeated substitution proves

 integral_G h(z)dz=integral_((0,1)^k)h(Z(r)) J_Z(r)dr,
 J_Z=product_i[(partial_i X_i+partial_i Y_i)/2].             (11)

The diagonal determinant inequality (equivalently Holder for two terms)
and (9) yield

 J_Z >= J[(q(L_A(X))^(-1/k)+q(L_B(Y))^(-1/k))/2]^k.          (12)

For clarity, the two-term Holder inequality says
product_i(u_i+v_i)^(1/k)>=product_i u_i^(1/k)
+product_i v_i^(1/k) for positive u_i,v_i; raising to k and
dividing by 2^k gives precisely the inequality used here.

## 5. Pointwise source domination and sharp cost

Write R_A(r)=R(L_A(X(r))), R_B(r)=R(L_B(Y(r))). Combining the actual
midpoint identity (5), scalar inequality (8), and (12) gives pointwise
on the open cube

 f(L_K(Z(r))) J_Z(r) >= J[R_A(r)+R_B(r)]/2.                 (13)

Define

 zeta=Z_#( J(R_A+R_B)dr/2 ).                               (14)

Its density on G is J(R_A+R_B)/(2J_Z) through the inverse map, and zero
off G. Formula (13) proves zeta<=f(L_K)H_k|F_K because G is contained
in the actual midpoint face. Using the endpoint marginals (10),

 J integral R_A dr=integral_(F_A)q(L_A)R(L_A)=A(t*),
 J integral R_B dr=B(t*).

This proves (4) and (3). All inequalities are measure inequalities, not
only total integrals.

The factor 2 in (3) is sharp, including genuine a!=0. For example take
F_A=F_B=F_K=F in one common hyperplane and any nonzero a and y for which
(2) holds on F. Symmetry and convexity make t*=0 a minimizer, and
A(0)+B(0)=2M. Translated identical faces with the corresponding affine
offsets give the same equality.
This also occurs for an actual projective normalizer: take A=B=K to be
one polytope and choose an interior source y different from its centroid.
Its projective normalizer is nonzero (the objective's derivative at a=0
is a nonzero multiple of g_K-y), and every common facet has this equality.

## 6. Exact all-cap identity and its two defects

Place the faces at actual bases -1,0,1, or at any two bases with their
midpoint as source. For any ambient affine cap margins ell_A,ell_B,ell_K
with

 ell_K((x+x')/2)=[ell_A(x)+ell_B(x')]/2,

let I_A(r),I_B(r),I_K(r) be their captured indicators under the same
maps X,Y,Z. Closed caps satisfy pointwise

                 I_A+I_B>=I_K.                           (15)

Define the actual endpoint weighted capture cost

 C_H=integral_(F_A) f(L_A)1_H
              +integral_(F_B) f(L_B)1_H
     =J integral(R_A I_A+R_B I_B)dr.                       (16)

Put l=(R_A+R_B)/2 and Delta=(R_A-R_B)/2. The exact identity is

 C_H=zeta(H)+J integral l(I_A+I_B-I_K)dr
                    +J integral Delta(I_A-I_B)dr.         (17)

The middle term is nonnegative; the last term retains the actual
correlation between denominator imbalance and the endpoint cap bits.
In particular

 C_H >= zeta(H)- (J/2) integral |R_A-R_B| I_K dr.            (18)

Indeed (15) and positivity give
R_A I_A+R_B I_B>=min(R_A,R_B)I_K, which is (18).
If mu_K=f(L_K)H_k|F_K, this becomes the exact-defect lower bound

 C_H >= mu_K(H)-(mu_K-zeta)(H)
                     -(J/2)integral |R_A-R_B|I_K dr.       (19)

The final defect is the integral against zeta over its captured image
of |R_A-R_B|/(R_A+R_B), a number in [0,1). The other defect is the
actual nonnegative uncovered source measure. Neither defect is given
an unproved uniform bound. Formula (17) can retain useful surplus that
the simpler (18) drops.

This ONE coupling and ONE dominated measure satisfy (17)--(19) for
every closed ambient halfspace simultaneously, including oblique
integer/continuous normals. They also retain the joint signature of
every finite cap menu; the maps were not reoptimized separately for
different caps.

For physical erosion losses, use the inward trace convention on a
whole supporting-facet coincidence. Translate X,Y,Z by the same
positive infinitesimal inward normal displacement, so their midpoint
identity persists, and take the pointwise limit of the indicators.
Every such limit exists; (15) remains true. Equations (16)--(19) then
hold for these inward selectors with the SAME unchanged coupling and
densities. In those formulas zeta(H) and mu_K(H) then mean the corresponding
selector integrals; at a whole-face supporting coincidence they need not
equal the measures of the literal closed trace. A proper tangent boundary
is null, and a pure-integer cap
has constant indicators, including its closed boundary bit. Thus no
positive boundary mass is silently replaced by an open cap.

## 7. Actual finite-normal implementation and limits of the conclusion

For a!=0 and finitely many distinct active contact normals, choose one
minimizing scalar t at each normal. Extend these finitely many values
to a bounded continuous scalar field on the sphere (disjoint small
neighborhood bump functions suffice). The corresponding continuous
fields c_A(n)=y+t(n)a/||a||^2, c_B(n)=2y-c_A(n) are admissible in the
actual two-input erosion from
`candidate 4283399302c56a21`,
Section 5. Its convexity/Jensen proof gives actual midpoint compatibility.
At every selected facet its weighted costs and cap losses are exactly
those above, multiplied by the source support distance H(n)>0.

This observation realizes the finitely specified choices; it does not
claim optimality at unselected normals, a simultaneous source choice,
or a global mixed-integer budget inequality.

The restriction on actual center shifts at a=0 is substantive. In
d=3, take parallel square faces with side lengths 1 and 3, and their
midpoint square of side 2. Take delta=1. For the constant density f(1)=1,
the unshifted endpoint cost is 10 while twice the source cost is 8.
Changing geometric centers cannot change a zero-vector denominator.
The analytic scalar shifts in (3) are therefore not available from
centers in this example. This is a scope calibration, not a failure
of (3) or of the a!=0 theorem.

There is a DISTINCT geometric implementation which does allow a=0.
The proved construction in
`candidate 6748c967393345b9`, Section 2,
permits the affine base denominator

                 1+a.(x-y)+b(n).(z-p).

At a midpoint triple z=p-v,p,p+v, take b(n).v=t*(n). This produces exactly
the two shifted denominators above, independently of whether a is zero.
Its global convex cuts retain all anchored compatibility relations and
charge only actual contacts; the present theorem applies at a tight
contact with positive endpoint facet measures. Finitely many desired
values of b(n).v can again be extended continuously. No simultaneous
optimization of incompatible prescriptions for several pairs is asserted.
For the square example with a=0, the allowed scalar minimum occurs at
t*=sqrt(3)-1: its endpoint cost is 4sqrt(3)-2<8. This is a valid affine
BASE shift, not a center shift when a=0.

## 8. Source surplus controls the denominator defect quadratically

The same proof supplies an explicit strengthening. Put

                  c_d=(d+1)/(3d-1)>0.

For the scalar data in (8), let l=[R(x)+R(y)]/2 and
D=[R(x)-R(y)]/2. Then

 f((x+y)/2)[(q(x)^(-1/k)+q(y)^(-1/k))/2]^k
                       >= l+c_d D^2/l.                    (20)

First, for z>0 and |r|<z,

 [((z+r)^p+(z-r)^p)/2]^k
       >= z^(d+1)[1+C_d(r/z)^2],
 C_d=(d+1)/(d-1),  p=(d+1)/(d-1).                          (21)

For d=2, p=3 and the inner even mean is 1+3(r/z)^2 exactly.
For d>=3, 1<p<=2; the second derivative of
[(1+u)^p+(1-u)^p]/2 is at least p(p-1), because the even average of
(1+u)^(p-2) and (1-u)^(p-2) is at least one by convexity.
Twice integrating from zero proves an inner lower bound
1+p(p-1)u^2/2. Raising to the integer k>=1 and using Bernoulli proves
(21), since kp(p-1)/2=C_d.

If x,y>=delta, divide (21) by their mean to the dth power; here l is
that mean and |D| is the half difference. This proves (20) even with
the larger constant C_d.

In the remaining case write x=delta-2s, y=delta+2r, with r>=s>=0,
and z=delta+r. The actual mean is z-s>=delta, while

 l=z+ds,  D=ds-r.

Applying (21) to delta,y and dividing by (z-s)^d gives a lower bound

 z(1-s/z)^(-d)[1+C_d r^2/z^2]
 >=z+ds+[C_d r^2+d(d+1)s^2/2]/z.                          (22)

The last step uses the quadratic Taylor lower bound for (1-u)^(-d)
on 0<=u<1; its second derivative is at least d(d+1).
Weighted Cauchy--Schwarz gives

 (r-ds)^2 <=[C_d r^2+d(d+1)s^2/2]
             [1/C_d+2d/(d+1)]
           =[C_d r^2+d(d+1)s^2/2]/c_d.

Since l>=z, (22) proves (20). Thus the tangent continuation has been
included in the quantitative bound as well.

Define on G, through the unique inverse Z, the measurable ratio

              kappa=|R_A-R_B|/(R_A+R_B).

Combining (20) with the actual Jacobian lower bound proves the measure
inequality

          mu_K-zeta >= c_d kappa^2 zeta.                   (23)

There is no density to specify outside G for kappa; set it to zero.
For every Borel E in the source face, Cauchy--Schwarz gives

 integral_E kappa d zeta
       <=sqrt[zeta(E)(mu_K-zeta)(E)/c_d].                 (24)

Consequently the SAME physical cap coupling gives

 C_H >=max{0, zeta(H)
                  -sqrt[zeta(H)(mu_K-zeta)(H)/c_d]}.      (25)

The stronger exact signed identity (17) remains available. Formula
(25) controls one defect by an actual source surplus; it does not bound
that surplus from above or assert that the resulting row pays a mixed
depth target.

At the level of total costs, let C=A(t*)+B(t*)>0. Applying (23) and
Cauchy--Schwarz to the signed denominator difference gives

 M >= C/2+c_d[A(t*)-B(t*)]^2/(2C)
   =(1+c_d)C/2-c_d Harm(A(t*),B(t*)).                     (26)

Indeed A-B=J integral(R_A-R_B)dr, while zeta has density Jl on the
cube and mass C/2. This proves the first inequality in (26); the second
line is the identity Harm(A,B)=C/2-(A-B)^2/(2C).
The coefficient c_d is explicit and sufficient; its optimality is not
claimed. The leading sharp cost bound (3) is unchanged.

## 9. Exact constant-source specialization for affine base shifts

Suppose a=0 and delta=1, so the source density is one. Let the endpoint
facet areas be alpha>=beta>0 and put u=(alpha/beta)^(1/(d+1))>=1.
Assign denominator u to the larger face and 2-u to the smaller face.
Their derivative masses both equal beta: q(u)alpha=beta and
q(2-u)beta=beta. Convexity and (6) therefore certify the exact optimum

 min(A+B)=beta[(d+1)u-(d-1)].                              (27)

The effective denominators are u and du-d+1, respectively. In this
case the coupling has uniform endpoint marginals and a constant ratio

 kappa=(d-1)(u-1)/[(d+1)u-(d-1)] < (d-1)/(d+1).            (28)

The exact constant is zero when u=1. Since u is the smaller effective
denominator, the same physical cap coupling yields

 C_H >= [2u/((d+1)u-(d-1))] zeta(H).                       (29)

Equations (27)--(29) are realized by the affine BASE shift of Section 7,
including its tangent branch when u>1. They are not generated by
moving centers when the projective vector vanishes. They make no
claim that this two-input choice is cheaper than the previously proved
one-input allocation, or that its cap credit alone pays a global row.

## 10. Exact limit of scalar integration: a local missed-cap example

The scalar conclusions alone cannot prove a Gamma_d/2 response bound.
Here is an actual planar-facet calibration, suggested by the parent
audit. Set d=2, a=0, delta=1, and identify the parallel faces by

 F_K=[0,1],  F_A=F_B=[0,21/40].

The minimizing shift is zero; all densities are one, M=1, A=B=21/40.
The identity coupling has zeta=Lebesgue measure on [0,21/40], and
kappa=0. Take the source and endpoint cap trace [5/9,infinity). Its
source weighted capture is 4/9=Gamma_2, its two endpoint captures are
zero, and zeta is entirely missed. The missed-source mass is 5/9,
which exceeds Harm(A,B)=21/40, so the earlier harmonic residual bound
also holds. Every conclusion (3)--(29) is respected.

The total source-plus-endpoint cost is 41/20, while the captured cost
is only 4/9. The Gamma_2/2 target times that total is 41/90, larger by
exactly 1/90. Thus even the quadratic denominator-defect control cannot
pay this row from scalar masses: its denominator defect is zero and
the obstruction is entirely the actual source measure outside zeta.

This local contact can be embedded in actual three-fiber convex bodies:
take K=[0,1]x[-1,1], A=B=[0,21/40]x[-1,1], at bases -1,0,1.
The middle is centrally symmetric about y=(1/2,0), so its projective
normalizer is a=0. The top faces give the displayed contact. The
ambient cap x_1-x_2/18>=1/2 passes through (0,y); on every top face
its trace is x_1>=5/9. Convex midpoint compatibility is immediate from
A=B subset K, and the convex hull of these three fibers has exactly
these integer fibers. Other normal faces contribute different physical
credits. In particular this is NOT an all-normal critical-circuit
counterexample and is not a counterexample to OC.

A global improvement therefore needs actual relations among the full
normal/cap profiles. Replacing that requirement by an unproved assertion
that zeta captures a fixed fraction of each source cap would discard
precisely the positive-measure deficit in this example.
